newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Lifeless Australian stocks limp to flat finish.
newsitem.headline: Lifeless Australian stocks limp to flat finish.

text.p: A lifeless Australian share market limped to a flat finish on Tuesday after a directionless day.
The All Ordinaries index struggled 1.6 points higher to 2,707.6, never venturing out of a tight 6.5 point band in a day where most participants were just not interested.
Emphasising the lack of interest was a turnover by value of just A$467 million, a level usually seen over the Christmas-New Year hiatus than in the normal course of business.
"It's like people are still on holidays," said Hartley Poynton broker Robin Forbes, referring to Monday's bank holiday in New South Wales.
Others shared similar sentiments, suggesting many traders were unlkely to take positions ahead of the plethora of profit reports starting to hit the market.
"People are not committed to go one way or the other," said Henderson Charlton Jones dealer Brett O'Donovan.
"They are waiting for profit results to come out in the near term. That may give us a lead one way or the other," he said.
Major miner Rio Tinto was the only interest in the majors, losing nearly one percent to A$20.48 (US$15.16).

Brokers noted the announcement of Australian unit managing director Ian Gould's departure to join Normandy Mining but said the global mining giant had also been weaker in London trading in recent days.
"It's been off a little in London in the last couple of days but maybe some people are concerned over his going. It's been a thin day though," said a Sydney broker.
With the upper echelon failing to excite much interest, the second tier was in the spotlight as profit numbers trickled in.

Wesfarmers was the star among the profit reporters, leaping 51 cents or over four percent to A$12.60 after posting a 50 percent increase in net profit to A$139.55 million for the 12 months to June 30.
The agricultural, energy and hardware group said its upbeat performance should continue, with further growth in revenue and earnings expected in the 1997/98 financial year.
"The report was fairly optimistic for future capital investment and growth," said Hartley Poynton's Forbes.
Manufacturer Pacific BBA ended six cents higher at A$5.70 after reporting a 27 percent higher half year net profit of A$12.6 million and predicting a stronger second half.

Retailer Just Jeans Holdings dropped 7.4 percent to A$1.50 early, its lowest level since October 1993, following a profit warning after the market close on Monday. But the shares recovered some ground to close seven cents down at A$1.55.

Just Jeans said pre-tax profit would be 65 percent lower in the year to end-July than in the previous corresponding period, citing poor merchandise decisions and exceptionally difficult apparel retailing conditions for the earnings slump.

Nickel producer QNI lost 10 to A$2.40 after the independent expert's report on its Gencor merger plan found the deal to be fair and reasonable. Under the deal, QNI is to issue 455.8 million new shares to Gencor's base metals arm Billiton Plc, representing 52.5 percent of the enlarged QNI. The capital return to shareholders would be 30 cents per share, compared with 28 cents previously.

Elsewhere, upmarket retailer David Jones Ltd ended a cent lower at A$1.88 after reporting marginally lower sales of A$1.44 billion for the 52 week period to July 26. The company said sales in the fourth quarter had improved.
Falls outnumbered rises by a ratio of about nine to eight, while about 29 percent of stocks traded remained steady. \
